wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e111.summary: Poses the sixth question of the Prologue: whether only a proposition that is per se in the second mode (where a property is predicated of its subject) can be the object of knowledge (scientia) in the strict sense.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e120.summary: Opening objection against the restriction: Aristotle (Posterior Analytics I) holds that where predicates are essentially ordered, the highest can be demonstrated of the lowest through the intermediate (e.g. 'substance' of 'man' through 'animal'); such a conclusion is per se in the first mode, so first-mode propositions can be demonstrated and known.
claims: Where predicates are essentially ordered, a higher predicate can be shown of the lowest through a middle term.
Such a demonstrated proposition is per se in the first mode.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e131.summary: Argument for the affirmative ('contra'): the conclusion of a demonstration is per se but not in the first mode, since according to Metaphysics VI there is no demonstration of substance or of what a thing is, and every first-mode predicate expresses the substance of the thing.
claims: There is no demonstration of substance or of the quod quid est.
Every first-mode predicate signifies the substance of the thing.
Hence demonstrative conclusions are not first-mode per se propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e142.summary: Lays out the two-part plan of the answer: first, what a second-mode per se proposition is; second, whether every demonstrable proposition is per se in the second mode.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e150.summary: Opens the first article with the thesis that every necessary proposition is per se in the first or the second mode. Propositions that are only necessary per accidens (such as many about the past, which became necessary contingently) are set aside. Every other necessary proposition can be evidently known, so there is a truth-bearing habit for it, and such habits concern only per se propositions, since both principles and conclusions are per se.
claims: Every simply necessary proposition is per se in the first or second mode.
Propositions about the past may be necessary only per accidens.
Every simply necessary proposition can be evidently known and so is the object of some truth-bearing habit.
Truth-bearing habits about the necessary concern only per se propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e176.summary: A second argument for the thesis from Posterior Analytics I (chapter on per se): Aristotle calls predicates that inhere in neither per se mode 'accidents', meaning they are predicated contingently. So any proposition that is neither first- nor second-mode per se is contingent, at least for proper predication. Ockham adds a qualification: if 'accident' meant real accidents, the claim would be false, since real accidents can be predicated per se in the second mode, at least in modal or equivalent propositions ('the moon is illuminable by the sun').
claims: Whatever is predicated in neither per se mode is predicated contingently, given proper predication.
Real accidents can be predicated per se in the second mode, at least in propositions de possibili.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e209.summary: A third supporting argument from Posterior Analytics I.6: whatever is predicated of something is predicated in the first mode, the second mode, or per accidens; accidental predicates are not necessary; so every necessary predicate is predicated per se in the first or second mode.
claims: Every predicate is predicated in the first mode, the second mode, or per accidens.
Accidental predications are not necessary.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e222.summary: Raises a difficulty for the thesis: 'matter is in potency to form' seems necessary. It cannot be first-mode per se, because neither a definition nor part of one is predicated. Nor can it be second-mode, because then form would be a property (passio) of matter, which is false since a subject is more perfect than its property and not the other way round.
claims: 'Matter is in potency to form' does not predicate a definition or part of a definition.
A subject is more perfect than its property.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e235.summary: First reply to the difficulty: 'matter is in potency to form' is per se because it belongs to demonstration as a principle or a conclusion. The same holds for every simply necessary proposition, since every such proposition belongs to demonstration.
claims: Whatever belongs to demonstration as principle or conclusion is per se.
Every simply necessary proposition belongs to demonstration.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e246.summary: Considers a further objection: then 'every man can be white', 'every fire is hot' and similar propositions would be per se, and contraries ('can be white', 'can be black') would be predicated per se of the same subject. Ockham accepts this consequence and says there is nothing unfitting about contraries being per se predicated of one subject in modal or equivalent propositions. He then reopens the question of which mode 'matter is in potency to form' reduces to.
claims: Contraries can be predicated per se of the same subject in propositions de possibili.
Propositions such as 'every man can be white' are per se.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e269.summary: Gives two accounts of the per se modes. On the first, which Ockham favors, a first-mode predicate imports nothing wholly extrinsic to what the subject signifies (only per se superiors and intrinsic parts). A second-mode predicate imports something really distinct from what the subject signifies ('every man is risible', 'God is creative'), so 'matter is in potency to form' is second-mode. The second account, apparently Lincolniensis (Grosseteste), makes predication first-mode when the predicate is a cause of the subject and second-mode when the subject causes the predicate. Ockham shows this yields awkward results: the matter–form proposition and its converse would both be first-mode, or the same proposition would fall under both modes, since matter and form are mutual causes.
claims: On the first account, first-mode predicates import only per se superiors or intrinsic parts of the subject.
On the first account, second-mode predicates import something really distinct from what the subject signifies.
'Matter is in potency to form' is per se in the second mode on the first account.
The causal account of the modes makes one proposition both first- and second-mode when the terms are mutual causes.
concepts: mutual causality of matter and form

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e319.summary: Qualifies the preceding account: whichever way the two modes are distinguished, the account applies only to purely affirmative propositions. Negative propositions such as 'no man is an ass' are per se in the first mode even though the predicate neither expresses the subject's essence nor causes it.
claims: The definitions of the per se modes apply to purely affirmative propositions.
A negative proposition like 'no man is an ass' is per se in the first mode.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e332.summary: Second article: whether every demonstrable proposition is second-mode per se. Ockham distinguishes a strict and a broad sense of 'demonstrable'. In the broad sense (any doubtful proposition that can be made evident through evident necessary premises arranged in mode and figure, the sense of scientia contrasted with intellectus and common to demonstration quia and propter quid), not every demonstrable proposition is second-mode. Some first-mode propositions, like 'every ass is an animal', can be doubtful and made evident through a middle term such as 'whatever moves itself is an animal'.
claims: 'Demonstrable' can be taken strictly or broadly.
In the broad sense, any doubtful proposition that can be made evident through evident necessary premises in proper syllogistic form is demonstrable.
Some first-mode per se propositions are doubtful and can be demonstrated in the broad sense.
Not every broadly demonstrable proposition is per se in the second mode.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e367.summary: Raises an objection to the preceding: Aristotle (Posterior Analytics) seems to prove that not everything syllogized from true, indemonstrable and immediate premises is demonstrated.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e374.summary: Replies that such first-mode propositions are not demonstrated by the most perfect demonstration (demonstratio potissima), just as demonstration quia is not potissima. They are still known by scientia proprie dicta, in the sense in which science is distinguished from understanding. Ockham conjectures that in the strict sense a proposition predicating a substantial subaltern genus of a lower genus can perhaps never be evidently known unless all species under the subject genus are known, so no such proposition could be strictly demonstrated.
claims: First-mode per se propositions are not demonstrated by demonstratio potissima.
Such propositions can still be known by scientia proprie dicta as distinguished from intellectus.
Perhaps a proposition predicating a higher genus of a lower genus cannot be evidently known without knowing all the species under the lower genus.

wo8uy7-d1e130-d1e394.summary: Answers the principal argument: in that passage Aristotle extends 'demonstration' to every syllogism from necessary and prior premises, but not every such syllogism is a demonstration. There is no demonstration when the conclusion is not doubtful, and a syllogism demonstrates only when the conclusion can be known through the premises, that is, when knowledge of the premises causes knowledge of the conclusion. Premises that are true, first, immediate and prior but do not cause knowledge of the conclusion do not make a demonstration.
claims: Not every syllogism from necessary and prior premises is a demonstration.
A syllogism whose conclusion is not doubtful is not a demonstration.
Demonstration requires that knowledge of the premises cause knowledge of the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e130.summary: Prologue question 6 asks whether only second-mode per se propositions are strictly knowable (scientia proprie dicta). Ockham first argues that every simply necessary proposition (excluding those necessary only per accidens) is per se in the first or second mode. He defends a semantic account of the modes: first-mode predicates import nothing wholly extrinsic to the subject's significate, while second-mode predicates import something really distinct. He prefers this to a causal account attributed to Grosseteste, admits per se predication of contraries in modal propositions, and treats negative propositions separately. He then distinguishes strict from broad demonstrability and argues that some first-mode propositions are doubtful and can be made evident through a middle term, so they are knowable by scientia, though not by demonstratio potissima. Since demonstration requires that knowledge of the premises cause knowledge of a doubtful conclusion, the answer to the question is negative in the broad sense of demonstration.
claims: Every simply necessary proposition is per se in the first or second mode.
The per se modes are best distinguished by whether the predicate imports something really distinct from what the subject signifies, not by causal relations.
Contraries can be predicated per se of one subject in propositions de possibili.
Not every demonstrable proposition, broadly taken, is per se in the second mode; some first-mode propositions are knowable by scientia.
Demonstration requires a doubtful conclusion whose knowledge is caused by knowledge of the premises.
